rejected.title: Consumers and online shopping
card: Scams
Fake websites, false sellers or fake offers can take a buyer's money and send nothing. The seller can be hard to identify or trace.
Overseas sellers
A seller based in another country may be hard to pursue. Australian courts and regulators may have limited power to enforce a remedy against it.
Data privacy
Online sellers collect personal details such as names, addresses and payment information. Consumers can lose control over how this data is stored, used or shared.
Online trade can change faster than legislation. The law is still catching up, so some gaps in protection remain.
rejected.remember: Online shopping brings extra risks, and the law is still catching up with them.

a.q: Priya pays for a jacket on a website based in another country. The jacket never arrives and the seller does not reply. Why is it hard for her to get a remedy?
opts: The seller is overseas, so enforcing a remedy is difficult
Online purchases are outside the reach of Australian law
Buyers cannot complain about sellers who trade online
Sellers must hold an Australian licence to trade online
a.why: A seller based overseas may be beyond the reach of Australian courts and regulators, so enforcing a remedy is hard. It is wrong to say no law applies to online purchases: the card says the law is still catching up, not that it is absent.
a.clue: Think about where the seller is based.

b.q: Tom buys shoes on a new website and receives them. Weeks later he gets many unwanted emails and calls from companies he has never dealt with. Which online shopping issue does this best show?
opts: Data privacy, as his details were shared or used
A scam, as the website took money and sent nothing
An overseas seller, as the site is based in another country
A gap in the law, as online sales have no rules at all
b.why: The unwanted contact suggests his personal details were stored, used or shared in ways he did not control, which is a data privacy issue. It is not a scam, because he received his shoes. Nothing says where the site is based, so it does not show an overseas seller.
b.clue: What did the website collect from Tom when he paid?

proposal.title: Consumers and online shopping
card: Scams
A fake website or a false offer can take a buyer's money and send nothing. The person behind it may be hard to identify or trace.
Overseas sellers
A seller based in another country can be hard to pursue. Australian courts and regulators may have limited power to make it provide a remedy.
Data privacy
Online sellers collect personal details such as names, addresses and payment information. Consumers can lose control over how that data is stored, used or shared.
Consumer law still protects people who buy online, but it can be hard to enforce. Online trade can change faster than the law, so some gaps in protection remain.
proposal.remember: Online shopping adds risks of scams, overseas sellers and misuse of personal data, and the law is still catching up.

a.q: Priya pays for a jacket on a website run from another country. It never arrives and the seller stops replying. Why might a remedy be hard to get?
opts: Regulators here may have little power over a foreign seller
Consumer law may not apply to goods bought online
Priya may not count as a consumer when buying online
Her personal data may have been shared without consent
a.why: The seller is based overseas, so Australian courts and regulators may struggle to make it provide a remedy. Consumer law still protects people who buy online, and Priya is still a consumer. The problem is enforcing the law, not whether it applies.
a.clue: Think about where the seller is based.

b.q: Tom buys shoes on a website and they arrive as ordered. Weeks later he gets many emails from companies he has never dealt with. Which issue does this best show?
opts: Data privacy, as his details reached other companies
A scam, as the website was set up to trick him
An overseas seller, as the companies are run from abroad
A scam, as the emails are offers he did not ask for
b.why: Companies he never dealt with have his details, so he has lost control over how his data was shared. That is a data privacy issue. It is not a scam in the card's sense, because he paid and the shoes arrived. Nothing in the case says anyone is based overseas.
b.clue: What did the website collect from Tom when he paid?
